card st-model-per-role  [decided]
Each pipeline agent runs on the model that its role needs
why: Most of the pipeline's cost comes from the agents that run many times per ticket: builder passes, reviewers and held-out runs. Opus stays where one mistake spreads to every later step or where a result is judged: the plan and the grader. The builder gets Sonnet with Opus as an advisor for the difficult parts, and the narrow or mechanical roles get Sonnet alone.

To keep cost down without weakening the gates, the pipeline picks the model of each agent from its role, not from one default.

| Role | Model |
| --- | --- |
| Spec writer, ticket writer | Opus |
| Grader | Opus |
| Builder | Sonnet, with Opus as advisor |
| Reviewers of each quality area | Sonnet |
| Held-out binder, step author | Sonnet |
| Overseer classifiers | Sonnet |

A role that is not in the table, such as the chat agent, keeps the default model of its own setting. The chat agent's model is chosen in the chat header (see #werk-model-select).

A weak builder result does not pass unseen: the grader and the checks still judge it on Opus. A weak plan has no such gate after it, so the planners stay on Opus.

card st-build-seam-role-env  [decided]
Each agent that the pipeline starts carries its role outside the prompt
why: One fake agent stands in for every agent in a test, so it must know which job each launch does. The prompt text changes often, so a fake that reads the prompt gives the wrong reply after a wording change. A role value in the environment of the launch stays fixed, and the real agent ignores it.

To pick a reply, a test fake must know which job a launch does: chat, build, grade, review, or another. The fake cannot see the caller. It sees only its own launch. One fake plays every agent at both test seams (see #werk-v0-seams), and the grader, the reviewers and the classifiers of a build are fakes too (see #st-build-seam).

So the pipeline puts a role name in the environment of every agent process it starts. A role name is a short fixed word for the job, such as builder or grader. The pipeline sets it in production a

**What it is.** Each agent that the pipeline starts carries a short fixed role name, such as `builder` or `grader`. This card gives names to three kinds of agent that had none:

- The held-out step author gets `step-author`.
- The held-out binder gets `binder`.
- The overseer classifiers get `classifier`.

Each of the three runs on Sonnet with no advisor.

**Why it matters.** Two things read the role name:

1. **Model choice.** #st-model-per-role picks the model from the role. An agent with no role name has no row in the table. It falls back to the default model, so a cheap Sonnet job could run on a more costly model without notice.
2. **Test fakes.** #st-build-seam-role-env makes the fake agent pick its scripted reply from the role. A launch with no role gets no scripted reply. A test of the held-out stage or the overseer cannot run.

**State.** The card is a proposal. The table on #st-model-per-role already lists "Held-out binder, step author" and "Overseer classifiers" as Sonnet. The only new fact here is the three fixed names.

card st-build-seam-role-env  [decided]
Each agent that the pipeline starts carries its role outside the prompt
why: One fake agent stands in for every agent in a test, so it must know which job each launch does. The prompt text changes often, so a fake that reads the prompt gives the wrong reply after a wording change. A role value in the environment of the launch stays fixed, and the real agent ignores it.

To pick a reply, a test fake must know which job a launch does: chat, build, grade, review, or another. The fake cannot see the caller. It sees only its own launch. One fake plays every agent at both test seams (see #werk-v0-seams), and the grader, the reviewers and the classifiers of a build are fakes too (see #st-build-seam).

So the pipeline puts a role name in the environment of every agent process it starts. A role name is a short fixed word for the job, such as builder or grader. The pipeline sets it in production and in tests alike. The real agent does not read it, so the value changes nothing in production. The fake reads it and picks the reply that the test scripted for that role. A new kind of agent gets a new role name when it is added.

Example:

- A test scripts reply R1 for the role builder and reply R2 for the role grader.
- The builder prompt opens with "Implement the ticket". The grader prompt opens with "Grade the change".

1. The pipeline starts the builder with the role builder. The fake reads builder and plays R1.
2. The pipeline starts the grader with the role grader. The fake reads grader and plays R2.
3. A later change rewords the builder prompt to "Build the ticket". The role stays builder. The fake still plays R1, and no test changes.

```
pipeline                      fake agent            script
--------                      ----------            ------
start(role=builder,
      "Build the ticket") --> reads role=builder -> R1
start(role=grader,
      "Grade the change") --> reads role=grader  -> R2

role=   the role name in the environment of the launch
R1, R2  the replies the test scripted for each role
```

card st-build-seam-role-env-reviewer-area  [decided]
Each reviewer's role name carries its quality area
why: The reviewers of a pass run at the same time, one per quality area, so a test cannot tell them apart by launch order or by prompt text. A test must still script a finding for one area only. A role name per area lets the fake give each reviewer its own reply.

A reviewer's role name is the word reviewer, a dash, and a short fixed word for its quality area (see #lp-prod-review for the areas): reviewer-design, reviewer-security, and so on. A new area gets a new role name when it is added. Every reviewer still lives for one pass, like every agent that is not a chat agent (see #werk-chat-fake-role).

Example:

- A test scripts reply F, one HIGH finding, for reviewer-security. It scripts reply E, with no finding, for every other area.

1. The pass starts one reviewer per area, all at once. Each carries its own reviewer-<area> name.
2. The fake reads reviewer-security and plays F. The other reviewers play E.
3. The pass fails at the review, and the failure names the security finding.
4. If the test scripts E for every area, no reviewer finds anything, and the pass goes green at the review.

```

reviewer-maintainability  -> E
reviewer-tests            -> E
reviewer-security         -> F (HIGH)  -> pass red at review

card st-build-seam-role-env-reviewer-area  [decided]
Each reviewer's role name carries its quality area
why: The reviewers of a pass run at the same time, one per quality area, so a test cannot tell them apart by launch order or by prompt text. A test must still script a finding for one area only. A role name per area lets the fake give each reviewer its own reply.

A reviewer's role name is the word reviewer, a dash, and a short fixed word for its quality area (see #lp-prod-review for the areas): reviewer-design, reviewer-security, and so on. A new area gets a new role name when it is added. Every reviewer still lives for one pass, like every agent that is not a chat agent (see #werk-chat-fake-role).

Example:

- A test scripts reply F, one HIGH finding, for reviewer-security. It scripts reply E, with no finding, for every other area.

1. The pass starts one reviewer per area, all at once. Each carries its own reviewer-<area> name.
2. The fake reads reviewer-security and plays F. The other reviewers play E.
card lp-prod-review  [decided]
The quality review
why: The grader asks only whether the diff does what the decided cards say. Nothing then catches a problem that no card names: duplication, weak tests, escape hatches, a new dependency.

Reviewer agents read the diff after the grader passes. They ask whether the change is good code. They do not ask whether the change is the right change. That is the grader's job (#lp-prod-judge). The two steps stay separate, so each one has one source of lines.

The review is part of the production rubric only. Prototype code does not get it (#lp-rubric-proto).

**The rubric is fixed and built into the tool**, the same for every project (#lp-rubric). It has five areas:

1. Design: module boundaries, coupling, error handling, fit with the code around it.
2. Maintainability: duplication, complexity, dead code, escape hatches such as type or lint suppressions and skipped tests.
card st-spec  [decided]
Plan ends with one spec per subtree, then tickets from the spec
why: A subtree holds many decisions, not one statement of the work. A spec puts the problem, the user stories, and the test seams in one agreed place. The tickets then split one whole.
subtree: 7 cards, 7 decided

The plan stage ends in two steps. `/to-spec` writes one spec over one decided subtree (#to-spec). `/to-tickets` then splits that spec into tickets (#to-tickets, #st-ticket).

One subtree gives one spec. One spec gives one or more tickets.

**An agent answers the skills' questions, not a person.** Both skills stop to ask: `/to-spec` asks whether the test seams are right, and `/to-tickets` asks about the granularity, the blocking edges, and the splits. The pipeline builds without a person, so an agent answers each question. It answers from the decided cards of the subtree and the map around it.

**An answer that no card gives becomes a card.** When the decided cards do not settle a question, the agent's answer is a new decision. It goes on the map under the subtree, so a person can see it and reopen it. It is never only in the spec.
card st-build-ticket  [decided]
The builder loop: one ticket, fresh passes until the checks, the grader, and the review pass
why: A fix is a new implement pass with the failure in its input, so the loop has no separate fix step.
subtree: 9 cards, 9 decided

One ticket, one worktree.

1. Implement. A fresh builder agent does one unit of work toward the ticket (#st-build-implement).
2. Check. The checks run: one command each, exit code only (#lp-checks).
3. Grade. A grader agent reads the diff against each decided card (#lp-prod-judge).
4. Review. Five reviewer agents, one per quality area, read the diff (#lp-prod-review).
